title: Spontaneously Formed CuSx Catalysts for Selective and Stable Electrochemical Reduction of Industrial CO2 Gas to Formate
abstract: The electrochemical CO2 reduction in aqueous media is a promising method for both the mitigation of climate changes and the generation of value-added fuels. Although many researchers have demonstrated selective and stable catalysts for electrochemical reduction of pure CO2 gas, the conversion of industrial CO2 gas has been limited. Here, we fabricated the copper sulfide catalysts (CuSx), which were spontaneously formed by dipping a Cu foil into a laboratory-prepared industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. Because industrial CO2 contains H2S gas, sulfur species dissolved in the electrolyte can easily react with the Cu foil. As the concentration of dissolved sulfur species increased, the reaction between the Cu foil and sulfur enhanced. As a result, the average size and surface density of CuSx nanoparticles (NPs) increased to 133.2 ± 33.1 nm and 86.2 ± 3.3%, respectively. Because of the larger amount of sulfur content and the enlarged electrochemical surface area of CuSx NPs, the Faradaic efficiency (FE) of formate was improved from 22.7 to 72.0% at −0.6 VRHE. Additionally, CuSx catalysts showed excellent stability in reducing industrial CO2 to formate. The change in FE was hardly observed even after long-term (72 h) operation. This study experimentally demonstrated that spontaneously formed CuSx catalysts are efficient and stable for reducing the industrial CO2 gas to formate.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: industrial CO2, H2S, copper, sulfide, CO2 reduction, formate

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into value-added chemicals using renewable electricity may effectively mitigate global climate changes.1−3 In this context, the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) has been attracting great attention because it can contribute to carbon sustainability.4−6
Previously, various metal electrodes have been examined as electrocatalysts for CO2RR in aqueous media. Au, Ag, Zn, Pd, and Ga are known for their high activity toward carbon monoxide (CO),7−14 and Sn, Pb, Bi, and Co can selectively generate formate (HCOOH).15−23 On the other hand, Cu has unique catalytic properties for producing multicarbon products, which cannot be produced with other transition metals.24−31 However, pristine Cu shows a large overpotential for CO2RR and high activity for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which compete with CO or formate production.30,31
Therefore, to improve the catalytic activity of Cu for CO2RR, various Cu-based catalysts such as nanoparticles (NPs),32−34
nanowires,35−37 and oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu)38−41 have been widely investigated. Despite many works of tuning the Cu electrodes,32−41 highly
selective catalysts have been demonstrated only in the electrolyte purged with pure CO2 gas. However, 40% of the total CO2 emission worldwide is emitted from the industry. 42 Accordingly, it is more efficient to directly reduce the industrial CO2 gas rather than pure CO2 for practical application. To reduce the industrial CO2 gas to value-added chemicals, it is necessary to know whether the catalytic properties are not degraded by unwanted reactions between the metal catalysts

and other products mixed in the industrial CO2 gas. Among the many gases mixed in industrial CO2 gas, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is known to poison the metal catalysts.
43−45 Sulfur impurities can easily activate the formation of sulfur compounds that suppress catalytic properties and stability. To solve this problem, many researchers have reported methods to remove the sulfur species in an electrochemical cell for decades.46−48 However, sulfur removal processes have the disadvantages of high operation cost, high temperature to decompose sulfur species, and production of other pollutants during the removal process.49 Therefore, we need to fabricate catalysts that maintained their stability and catalytic activities in sulfur-containing aqueous environments. Recently, copper sulfide (CuSx) catalysts have been studied because of their high selectivity for formate.50−57 Density function theory calculation demonstrated that the presence of sulfur species on Cu surface promotes adsorption of HCOO* intermediate but suppresses formation of *COOH intermediate. Therefore, the production of formate from HCOO* is favored; meanwhile, CO production through *COOH intermediate is inhibited.56 In spite of several works on CuSx catalysts for selective production of formate, it has not been studied whether CuSx catalysts can maintain their catalytic properties in an aqueous electrolyte containing H2S, which inevitably presents in the industrial CO2 gas. Herein, we fabricated CuSx catalysts prepared by dipping the Cu foil into a H2S-containing industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte and investigated their catalytic activity and stability toward CO2RR. To elucidate the relationship between the chemical composition of CuSx and its catalytic activity, catalysts with different amounts of sulfur species were prepared by varying the concentration of H2S in an electrolyte. As the concentration of H2S in an electrolyte increased, not only the size and surface density of CuSx NPs enlarged but also the amount of sulfur increased. As a result, CuSx catalysts improved FEHCOOH from 22.7 to 72.0% at −0.6 VRHE. Moreover, CuSx catalysts were stable during the 72 h operation in the industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on catalysts that exhibit both high formate selectivity and stability using industrial CO2 gas. This study provides guidelines to design the catalysts that work under an industry-applicable CO2 reduction electrolyte.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Preparation of an Extreme Flat Copper Film. Glass was used as a mother substrate for fabricating an extreme flat copper (EFCu) film.58 The mother substrate was cleaned sequentially with acetone, isopropyl alcohol, and deionized water (DI water). After surface cleaning, 100 nm thick Cu films were deposited by electron beam evaporation method with a rate of 0.1 nm/s to make Cu seed layers. The chamber pressure was maintained at about 1×10−6 Torr, and the substrate was held at room temperature. To electroplate a thick Cu foil, the cathode (100 nm thick Cu seed layers) and anode (bulk Cu stick) were electrically connected using a Keithley 2400 digital source meter to ensure a constant current density (20 mA/ cm2). During electroplating, the growth rate was about 50 μm/h, and the time was controlled to yield a final thickness of about 100 μm. The temperature of the electroplating solution was maintained to be 60 °C. Because of the large compressive stress between the thick Cu foil and the glass mother substrate, the Cu foils could easily be peeled off from the glass mother substrate. 2.2. Preparation of CuSx Catalysts. CuSx catalysts were fabricated by dipping the EF-Cu film into a laboratory-prepared industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte with different H2S
concentrations. Because the CO2 gas emitted from the industry contains H2, CO, CH4, and H2S gases, we demonstrated the laboratory-prepared industrial CO2 with two types of mixed gases. One is the CO2 gas that contains small amount of H2, CO, and CH4, and the other one is the H2S gas that contains 300 ppm of H2S and 99.97% N2. To prepare electrolytes that had different amounts of sulfur species, the electrolyte was saturated by CO2 gas before purging the H2S gas. Therefore, the pH value for the electrolyte at tpurge = 0 min is around 6.8. As the purging time of H2S gas increases from 0 to 90 min, the pH value was gradually increased from 6.77 to a saturated value of 7.46 (Figure S1). Five catalysts were prepared by changing the purging time from 0 to 40 min and denoted as Cu-0 min, CuSx-10 min, -20 min, -30 min, and -40 min.
2.3. Characterization. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy were performed using a PHILIPS XL30S with an accelerating voltage of 5 kV and a working distance of 6 mm. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using a Thermo ESCALAB250i X-ray photoelectron spectrometer at a base pressure of 1 × 10−9 Torr. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) was conducted at 200 kV with a Cs-corrector. To conduct the crosssectional TEM analysis, a focused ion beam (FIB) system was operated with a beam of 30 keV Ga+ ions to make cross-sectional CuSx catalysts. The average size and surface density of CuSx NPs was determined using a FIB−SEM analyzer and a computer-based image analyzer (Leopard 2009).
2.4. Electrochemical Measurements. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), electrochemical surface area (ECSA), Faradaic efficiency (FE), and current density were measured in the H-type cell separated by a Nafion membrane with a three-electrode system. Ag/AgCl electrodes filled with 3 M KCl were used as the reference electrode, and Pt mesh was used as the counter electrode. The electrolyte used for electrochemical measurements was an aqueous solution of 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.95%) prepared from dissolving the solid salt in DI water. The electrolyte was purged with N2 or industrial CO2 before measurements. The measured potential (VAg/AgCl) could be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE) using the Nernst equation: VRHE = VAg/AgCl + 0.222 + 0.0592 × pH. The EIS spectra were recorded in a frequency range from 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz at a potential of −0.6 VRHE with an amplitude of 30 mV. All the measurements were conducted under ambient pressure at room temperature.
2.5. Product Analysis. Gas products (CO, CH4, and H2) were analyzed with gas chromatography (Inficon, 3000 Micro GC) equipped with two thermal conductivity detectors connected to a Molsieve column and Plot U column. After the reaction, the gas products were pumped into the gas chromatograph for analysis. Samples were analyzed for each potential from −0.4 to −1.2 VRHE. Liquid products (formate) were analyzed using a 500 MHZ 1H 1D liquid NMR spectrometer (Bruker) at 25 °C. The standard solution consisted of 5 mM dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma-Aldrich) in D2O (Sigma-Aldrich) as a solvent. The amount of formate products was calculated by integrating areas of the products with that of dimethyl sulfoxide standard solution.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Control the Morphology of CuSx Catalysts. For the fabrication of CuSx catalysts using industrial CO2, EF-Cu films were dipped into a laboratory-prepared industrial CO2purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte with different H2S concentrations (Figure S2). Because the formation reaction of CuSx between the Cu and sulfur species has a negative Gibbs free energy of formation of −53.6 kJ/mol,59 CuSx could be spontaneously formed on the surface of EF-Cu films (Figure S3). The morphologies of CuSx catalysts with different amounts of sulfur species were characterized by top-view and cross-sectional SEM images (Figures 1a,b and S4). Small NPs
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c03606 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
were observed on the surface of Cu foil after CO2 reaction in a pure CO2-purged electrolyte (Figure 1a). On the other hand, large NPs were formed on the Cu surface exposed to a 40 min H2S-purged electrolyte (Figure 1b). To calculate the average size and surface density of NPs, FIB−SEM analysis and computer-based image analysis were conducted (Figures S5 and S6). As the H2S purging time (tpurge) in the electrolyte increased from 10 to 40 min, the average size of NPs gradually increased from 55.2 ± 15.3 to 133.2 ± 33.1 nm with an increased surface density from 23.4 ± 2.2 to 86.2 ± 3.3% (Figure 1c). It is evident that the higher concentration of H2S in the electrolyte causes the faster reaction of CuSx formation, accordingly, the larger particle size and the higher surface density. To characterize the atomic composition of CuSx NPs, EDX measurement was conducted (Figure 1d). Cu-0 min catalysts showed a strong Cu Lα line at 0.93 keV and an O Kα line at 0.52 keV. However, the S Kα line at 2.3 keV was not observed, indicating that these catalysts were composed of Cu and CuO NPs. On the other hand, the peak intensity of the S Kα line was gradually increased as the tpurge increased from 10 to 40 min. From these results, it is clearly demonstrated that the concentration of sulfur species plays a key role in determining the composition and morphology of CuSx NPs. 3.2. Crystal Structure and Atomic Composition of
CuSx Catalysts. To obtain insights into the material properties of CuSx catalysts, the crystal structure of the Cu-0 min catalysts (Figure 2a) and CuSx-40 min catalysts (Figure 2b) was characterized by a high-resolution transmission electron microscope. In the Cu-0 min catalysts, the HRTEM images and electron diffraction patterns of selected area showed d-spacings of 0.210 and 0.170 nm, corresponding to the Cu(111) and CuO (202) planes, respectively. On the other hand, the CuSx-40 min catalysts showed d-spacings of 0.210, 0.170, 0.180, and 0.320 nm, corresponding to the Cu(111), CuO (202), CuS (110), and CuS (101) planes, respectively.
This indicates that the CuSx catalysts are composed of three phases of Cu, CuO, and CuS. To identify the compositional distribution of Cu, S, and O in CuSx catalysts, we carried out elemental mapping using EDX coupled with high-angle annular dark-field imaging/scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF/STEM). The Cu-0 min catalysts
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c03606 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
showed a smooth surface without noticeable NPs (Figure 2c). Cu atoms were uniformly distributed on the entire Cu foil; meanwhile, the intensity of sulfur and oxygen is too low to distinguish each element from the background. On the other hand, large CuSx NPs were observed on the surface of CuSx-40 min catalysts (Figures 2d and S7). There was a clear intensity contrast of Cu and S at the boundary between the Cu foil and CuSx NPs; the intensity of Cu is lower and that of S was stronger on the CuSx NPs. We further conducted EDX-line scanning for Cu-0 min and CuSx-40 min catalysts (Figure S8). For Cu-0 min catalysts, strong Cu Kα was detected throughout the sample without noticeable detection of S Kα or O Kα lines. In contrast, the CuSx-40 min catalysts showed a less intensive Cu Kα line at the CuSx NPs than the Cu foil. In addition, S atoms were measured with a relatively stronger intensity than O atoms. Therefore, we concluded that the CuSx NPs were mainly composed of Cu with a small amount of S with a size of nearly 180 nm. This result is in good agreement with FIB− SEM analysis (Figure 1c). To quantify the atomic composition of prepared samples,
XPS was conducted (Figure 3). For elucidation of the bonding
state of copper and sulfur species on the surface, deconvolution of Cu 2p3/2 and S 2p was carried out with four and two binding states of Cu−OH (934.4 eV), Cu−O (933.0 eV), Cu−Cu (932.5 eV), Cu−S (931.9 eV), S−S (163.2 and 161.9 eV), and S−M (162.9 and 161.7 eV) (Figure 3a,b).60−62 The pristine Cu foil (before reaction) showed a strong metallic Cu−Cu bond without the presence of a Cu−S bond. However, CuSx (10−40 min) catalysts showed a Cu−S bond (Figure 3a). Similarly, the pristine Cu foil and Cu-0 min samples did not show S−S and S−M bonds in the S 2p spectrum, but CuSx (10−40 min) catalysts showed clear S−S and S−M bonds (Figure 3b). As the tpurge increases, the intensity of S−S and S− M bonds gradually increased because the higher concentration of H2S in the electrolyte provides more sulfur species on CuSx
NPs. On the other hand, there was no noticeable change of bonding state of oxygen in the O 1s spectrum (Figure S9). A small amount of O−M bonds at 530.4 eV are originated from the native copper oxide, formed during exposure to ambient air prior to XPS analysis. In the calculated elemental compositions of the CuSx catalysts (Table S1), the relative atomic ratio of S 2p/Cu 2p was gradually increased to a maximum value of 0.19 as the tpurge increases from 0 to 40 min. From these XPS results, we confirmed that CuSx NPs were spontaneously formed and the amount of sulfur gradually increased with the concentration of H2S in an electrolyte (Figure S10).
3.3. Electrochemical CO2 Reduction. Electrochemical CO2 reduction activities were evaluated by a cyclic voltammogram at the first scan of CuSx catalysts with various H2S concentrations tuned by changing the tpurge (Figure 4a). A strong cathodic peak at −0.4 VRHE in the first cycle corresponds to the reduction of CuS to CuSx. In the subsequent redox cycles, the peak of CuS disappeared (Figure S11). To observe the current density from CO2RR, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were plotted for the second cycle of CV scan in a N2-purged and industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a scan rate of 50 mV/s (Figure 4b). In the industrial CO2-purged electrolyte, the current density of CuSx catalysts was gradually increased with tpurge from −8.3 to −18.4 mA/cm2 at −1.4 VRHE. To verify the reason for the increased current densities, the electrochemical surface area of CuSx catalysts was measured via charge/discharge curves on a potential range from 0.35 to 0.45 VRHE for various scan rates (Figure S12). Then, the current density measured at 0.40 VRHE was plotted as a function of scan rate (Figure 4c). Because the slope of the current density-scan rates curve indicates a doublelayer capacitance that linearly correlates with the electrochemical surface area, the roughness of the electrocatalysts could be determined. The double-layer capacitance of CuSx-40 min catalysts (187.7 μF/cm2) was 2.1 times larger than that of Cu-0 min catalysts (91.5 μF/cm2), indicating that the surface area of the CuSx-40 min catalyst is at least 2 times larger than that of Cu-0 min catalysts. EIS measurements were conducted to investigate the kinetics of the electron-transfer process in the industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Figure 4d). The first semicircle at the high-frequency region indicates a capacitive/resistive behavior between the solution, reference electrode, and working electrode constituted by the samples. It has been known that the second semicircle in the lowfrequency region is the resistance from the charge transfer during an electrocatalytic reaction. From the results indicating that the radius of the second semicircle gradually decreased with the concentration of H2S, we believe that the CuSx NPs facilitate the charge transfer for the CO2 reduction. The FE (Figure S13) and partial current density (Figure
S14) of CuSx catalysts were measured at different applied potentials from −0.4 to −1.2 VRHE in an industrial CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. Cu-0 min catalysts mainly converted CO2 to carbon monoxide (CO) with an FECO of 39.8% at −0.8 VRHE (Figure 5a). However, the FECO of CuSx catalysts gradually decreased below 3% as the tpurge increases to 40 min. On the other hand, the maximum FEHCOOH dramatically increased from 22.7 to 71.8% at −0.6 VRHE (Figure 5b) because the larger amount of sulfur on CuSx catalysts can effectively suppress the HER from 43.6 to 16.8% (Figure S15). We plotted the partial current density and FEs of CO and formate at −0.6 VRHE as a function of tpurge in the electrolyte (Figure 5c). At −0.6 VRHE, FECO was drastically
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c03606 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
suppressed from 25.6 to 2.7%, and accordingly, the partial current density of CO also gradually decreased from 0.26 to 0.09 mA/cm2. Meanwhile, FEHCOOH gradually increased to a maximum value of 71.8%, and the partial current density of formate increased from 0.23 to 2.53 mA/cm2. Further increased tpurge longer than 40 min showed that the FEs and current densities of formate and CO were hardly changed (Figure S16a). Moreover, CuSx catalysts maintained similar morphologies regardless of tpurge in the electrolyte (Figure S16b), indicating that sulfur species are fully saturated in the 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte and does not affect the catalytic activity when tpurge ≥ 40 min. From these results, we believe that high FEHCOOH of CuSx catalysts was originated from a large amount of sulfur content together with increased particle size and surface density of CuSx NPs (Table S2). To identify whether CuSx catalysts that formed in industrial CO2 maintained their catalytic activities in the pure CO2-purged electrolyte, three different catalysts were evaluated as follows: (1) catalytic performance of Cu foil was characterized in the pure CO2-purged electrolyte; (2) CuSx catalysts evaluated in the industrial CO2-purged electrolyte; and (3) CuSx catalysts were prepared in the industrial CO2 electrolyte and then transferred to the pure CO2-purged electrolyte for the measurement (Figure 6). In the LSV curves, the CuSx catalysts prepared in the industrial CO2-purged electrolyte showed higher current densities (−18.4 and −17.1 mA/cm2) than that of the Cu foil (−8.2 mA/cm2) regardless of the electrolyte in which the measurement was conducted (Figure 6a). In the EIS
measurement, CuSx catalysts that were measured in pure CO2and industrial CO2-purged electrolytes revealed similar EIS spectra, while the Cu foil had a higher charge-transfer resistance (Figure S17). From this, we concluded that the kinetics of reductive reaction is dominated by the composition of catalysts, not by the presence of sulfur species in the electrolyte. Additionally, we compared FEHCOOH for prepared samples to identify whether the catalytic selectivity of CuSx catalysts was altered by the electrolyte (Figure 6b). The maximum FEHCOOH of the Cu foil measured in the pure CO2purged electrolyte was as low as 22.7% at −0.6 VRHE. However, it was remarkably increased to a maximum value of 71.8% for CuSx catalysts measured in industrial CO2-purged electrolytes. Interestingly, CuSx catalysts preserved their maximum FEHCOOH of 70.2% even in the pure CO2-purged electrolyte. Therefore, once CuSx catalysts were spontaneously formed, they are effective to reduce CO2 to formate in both pure CO2and industrial CO2-purged electrolytes.
3.4. Stability of CuSx Catalysts. For practical applications, the stability of CuSx catalysts is an important factor in industrial CO2-purged electrolyte. Therefore, the stability of CuSx-40 min catalysts was evaluated for 72 h at a constant potential of −0.6 VRHE. For the total current density measurement, industrial CO2 was kept bubbled in the electrolyte to prevent the changing of the pH value during the reaction. The total current density of CuSx catalysts was almost constant for 72 h, indicating that the electrochemical reaction was stable under long-term reaction (Figure 7a). The
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c03606 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
CuSx catalysts showed a formate FE of 73.1% at 12 h, and a slight change in FEHCOOH was observed after 72 h of reaction. The change of formate current densities was hardly observed with operation time for 72 h (Figure S18). Furthermore, the surface morphology of CuSx catalysts was preserved after the electrochemical reaction of 12, 36, and 72 h (Figure 7b). From the results that CuSx catalysts maintained their initial FEHCOOH and morphology, we concluded that CuSx catalysts are stable in the industrial CO2-purged electrolyte even after the longterm reaction. 3.5. Discussion. To date, much research effort has been
devoted to the development of high-performance catalysts, primarily carbon or Sn-based catalysts for CO2RR in aqueous solution (Table 1). Recent studies demonstrated that the introduction of heteroatoms such as nitrogen or boron into carbon materials could promote catalytic activity toward CO
or formate production.63−68 Also, many carbon-based catalysts were fabricated through a facile chemical synthesis under mild conditions.63−65 Most of the carbon-based catalysts reported in the literature are powders, which are coated onto the conductive substrates such as glassy carbon with the assistance of polymeric binders.66,68 However, the charge transfer between catalysts and substrate is inherently limited because of the presence of binders. In addition, the stability of the catalyst is relatively poor because the glued catalysts tend to be exfoliated from the substrates under vigorous gas evolution conditions. Sn-based catalysts showed comparable catalytic performance to carbon-based catalysts for FEHCOOH and effectively suppressed the HER.69−74 However, the carbonand Sn-based catalysts require a large overpotential to achieve the high selectivity of formate, thereby limit practical application for mass production. Recently, CuSx catalysts have been studied because of their high selectivity toward formate at moderate overpotential.53−57 Until now, several methods such as electrodeposition56 and solvothermal synthesis57 have been reported for fabrication of CuSx catalysts for selective production of formate. However, it is difficult to obtain reproducible CuSx catalysts by electrodeposition method because the morphology of CuSx is too sensitive to pH of the electrolytes and potentials. The solvothermal synthesis has problems of high temperature and binding processes to attach the catalysts to the conductive substrate.
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c03606 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
These complex manufacturing steps limit the production of low-cost catalysts. In addition, catalytic activities of previous CuSx catalysts were only evaluated in pure CO2-purged electrolytes. In this work, CuSx catalysts were spontaneously formed by a facile method of dipping Cu foil into the electrolytes purged with sulfur-containing industrial CO2. These CuSx catalysts revealed high formate selectivity not only in the pure CO2-purged electrolytes but also in the industrial CO2-purged one. To the best of our knowledge, this
is the first work that electrochemically converted industrial CO2 to formate with high selectivity and stability.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we fabricated highly selective and stable CuSx catalysts that reduce industrial CO2 to formate. The CuSx catalysts were spontaneously formed by dipping the Cu foil into an industrial CO2-purged electrolyte that contains H2S gas. We found that the spontaneous reaction between Cu foil and sulfur species occurred, and the average size and surface density of CuSx NPs increased with the concentration of H2S. As a result, the maximum FEHCOOH was improved from 22.7 to 71.8%. The CuSx catalysts were also very effective to produce formate in both industrial CO2- and pure CO2-purged electrolytes and stable during long-term operation of 12 h. Until now, there was no effort to study the catalysts that reduce industrial CO2 because sulfur species in industrial gas can degrade the catalytic activities and stability. However, we successfully demonstrated highly active and stable CuSx catalysts for reducing industrial CO2 to formate. We believe that the synergistic effects of Cu and S species on CO2 reduction can be extended to the other Cu-based catalysts in the near future.
